Fortner ORCID: orcid.org/0000-0002-3669-779X 1 Show authors Nature Water ( 2026 ) Cite this article Save article View saved research 807 Accesses Metrics details Abstract Photo-driven, plasmon-enhanced catalysis enables polyfluoroalkyl and perfluoroalkyl substance (PFAS) degradation in water under ambient conditions. Here we show that ultraviolet (UV) irradiation-induced localized surface plasmon resonance drives reductive defluorination of perfluorooctanoic acid and perfluorooctane sulfonic acid, two legacy contaminants. Stable, quantum-sized palladium and platinum nanocatalysts supported on aminated mesoporous silica nanoparticles (MSN–NH 2 –Pd and MSN–NH 2 –Pt) transform perfluorooctanoic acid and perfluorooctane sulfonic acid with stoichiometric, or near-stoichiometric, fluoride release under low-intensity UVC or UVA irradiation at room temperature. Time-resolved 19 F nuclear magnetic resonance, high-resolution mass spectrometry and complementary analyses indicate a stepwise reductive hydrodefluorination pathway in which oxidized, short-chain products do not measurably accumulate under the conditions studied. Scavenger and control experiments are consistent with hydrated electrons and in situ hydrogen generation as key reactive species. Taken together, the results indicate that synergistic interfacial PFAS sorption, plasmon-induced hydrogen evolution and hydrated electron formation drive PFAS defluorination under mild reaction conditions. Environmental chemistry Environmental impact Pollution remediation Main Polyfluoroalkyl and perfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) represent a broad class of synthetic organic chemicals that contain a hydrophobic fluorinated carbon chain and a polar end group. Due to their amphiphilic properties and high stability, PFAS have been extensively used as surface coatings, and aqueous film-forming foams for fire suppression, among other widespread applications 1 , resulting in extensive environmental contamination 2 . Based on the highly recalcitrant nature of PFAS attributed to the strength of C–F covalent bonds (~485 kJ mol −1 ) and a large number of potential PFAS structures (~15,000) occurring at low environmental concentrations with documented human health risks, effective PFAS remediation remains an important and urgent global health need 3 , 4 , which is reflected in recent regulatory actions 5 . The treatment of PFAS contamination using conventional processes poses several challenges due to their highly stable chemical structure(s) 6 . The various technologies currently available to transform PFAS can be generally categorized as chemical/catalytic, plasma-based, thermal and bio-based 6 , 7 . Among these, chemical/catalytic transformation processes have proven effective for PFAS degradation via chemical oxidation and reduction, photocatalysis, electrocatalysis and sonolysis-based pathways 6 . Catalytic transformations have been demonstrated for a library of PFAS compounds with relatively lower energy/economic requirements compared with traditional methods, such as thermal degradation, and are characterized by rapid processes, unlike the slow (or limited) nature of biologically driven transformations 8 , 9 . From a sustainability perspective, photo-driven catalytic processes offer inherent advantages by reducing energy demands and chemical inputs. Recent advances in ultraviolet (UV) reactor design and light-emitting diode (LED) technology have significantly improved the scalability and energy efficiency of UV-based treatment systems, making them increasingly viable for scaled water treatment and environmental remediation 10 , 11 . Techno-economic analyses have further highlighted the potential cost-effectiveness of UV-driven approaches, particularly for decentralized or point-of-entry treatment scenarios compared with other emerging technologies 12 , 13 . Among photocatalytic strategies, plasmon-enhanced photocatalysis, a growing field focused on enabling/enhancing chemical reactions through specific light–matter interactions, is a powerful strategy for driving thermodynamically challenging reactions under ambient conditions 14 .
